## Overview

By the end of this lecture you can state the three results that carried this course from
a single unknown probability to a decision made under model uncertainty, and show, on one
dataset, exactly what each successive repair bought over the one before it.

::: {.callout-important}
## The result of this chapter

Every model in this course is the same four objects, in the same order,

$$
p(\theta) \quad\text{prior}, \qquad
p(y \mid \theta) \quad\text{likelihood}, \qquad
p(\theta \mid y) \;\propto\; p(y\mid\theta)\,p(\theta) \quad\text{posterior}, \qquad
p(y_\ast \mid y) = \int p(y_\ast \mid \theta)\, p(\theta \mid y)\, d\theta \quad\text{posterior predictive},
$$

whether $\theta$ is a single probability, a coefficient vector, or a whole vector
autoregression. The posterior is always this proportionality statement. The difficulty
the course spent fourteen weeks on is that the sums and integrals needed to summarise the
posterior, and above all the integral defining the posterior predictive, are almost never
available in closed form once $\theta$ has more than a couple of dimensions or more than
one model is on the table.
:::

After working through this chapter you can

1. state the four objects, prior, likelihood, posterior, posterior predictive, for a model
   given only its assumptions;
2. diagnose which of the course's three recurring difficulties, intractability, estimation
   error or identification and model error, a given empirical failure belongs to;
3. derive the general Normal-Inverse-Gamma posterior and read its mean as a
   matrix-weighted average of the prior mean and least squares;
4. derive the model-averaged posterior predictive and interpret posterior model
   probabilities and inclusion probabilities;
5. implement one conjugate model three ways, in closed form, by direct simulation and by
   a Gibbs sampler, and check that the three agree;
6. compare a single fitted model against a shrinkage prior and a model average on
   identical out-of-sample data, and rank them without flattering any of the three;
7. read a chapter's Discussion section as a record of what the course settled and what it
   left to judgement.

Week 15 of 15, the review, paired with the [Week 15 exercise
session](../exercise-sessions/15-review.qmd). The chapter assumes every earlier lecture
and introduces no new machinery; its only job is to run the whole chain once more, on one
dataset, from the same starting point as Lecture 1 to the same kind of decision as
Lectures 9 and 13.

## Motivation: one probability, then a decision under model uncertainty {#sec-motivation}

Lecture 1 began with a single unknown probability, whether next month brought a loss, and
turned it into a posterior over that one number by Bayes' theorem. Lecture 9 ended a very
different way, with a decision that had to be made without knowing which of several
models was right, so the decision used a predictive distribution averaged over all of
them. The whole course is the distance between those two moves. In between, the unknown
stopped being a single probability and became first a coefficient vector, then a vector of
coefficients too large for the sample to pin down, then a coefficient that changed every
month, then a variance that changed every month, then a set of models rather than one. At
every step the four objects of the Overview box stayed the same; what changed was what
$\theta$ was, and how hard the posterior and the posterior predictive were to get at.

Watch the first move happen on data before taking the rest on faith. Section 5 below
introduces this chapter's one dataset properly, a monthly panel used to forecast core
inflation a year ahead. Ask the Lecture 1 question of it directly: unconditionally, in how
many months of the last sixty-five years was inflation over the following twelve months
above three percent a year, a plausible line in the sand for a policy maker.

```{python}
#| label: fig-motivation-conditioning
#| fig-cap: "The probability that inflation over the next twelve months exceeds three percent, computed three ways: ignoring today's information, and conditioning on whether inflation over the past twelve months was above or below four percent."
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

DATA = next(p for p in (Path("data"), Path("../data")) if p.exists())
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.figsize": (7, 4.2), "axes.grid": True,
                     "grid.alpha": 0.3, "font.size": 11})

fred_c = pd.read_parquet(DATA / "fred_macro_monthly.parquet").dropna()
lpce, lip_c = np.log(fred_c["core_pce"]), np.log(fred_c["industrial_prod"])
panel_c = pd.DataFrame({
    "infl_next": 100 * (lpce.shift(-12) - lpce),
    "infl_past": 100 * (lpce - lpce.shift(12)),
    "unemp": fred_c["unemployment"],
    "spread": fred_c["yield_10y"] - fred_c["fed_funds"],
    "d_ff": fred_c["fed_funds"].diff(12),
    "ipg": 100 * (lip_c - lip_c.shift(12)),
    "y10": fred_c["yield_10y"],
}).dropna()

thr = 3.0
p_naive = float((panel_c["infl_next"] > thr).mean())
hi_mask = panel_c["infl_past"] > 4.0
p_hi = float((panel_c.loc[hi_mask, "infl_next"] > thr).mean())
p_lo = float((panel_c.loc[~hi_mask, "infl_next"] > thr).mean())

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
bars = ax.bar(["unconditional\n(all 774 months)",
               "recent inflation\nabove 4%  (n=221)",
               "recent inflation\nat or below 4%  (n=553)"],
              [p_naive, p_hi, p_lo], color=["grey", "firebrick", "steelblue"])
ax.set_ylabel("share of months with inflation above 3% next year")
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.05)
for b, v in zip(bars, [p_naive, p_hi, p_lo]):
    ax.text(b.get_x() + b.get_width() / 2, v + 0.02, f"{v:.3f}", ha="center")
ax.set_title("One number hides what the data are ready to say")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"unconditional P(inflation next year > 3%) = {p_naive:.3f}")
print(f"conditional on recent inflation above 4%:  {p_hi:.3f}  (n = {hi_mask.sum()})")
print(f"conditional on recent inflation at or below 4%: {p_lo:.3f}  (n = {(~hi_mask).sum()})")
```

The unconditional share is $0.437$, a Beta-Binomial calculation exactly like Lecture 1's,
treating every month as an exchangeable draw from one fixed probability. It is not wrong,
but it is not what a forecaster standing in a particular month wants, because it throws
away everything known about that month. Split the sample by whether inflation over the
past year was already running above four percent and the single number comes apart:
$0.964$ of the months that started hot stayed above three percent, against $0.226$ of the
months that did not. The unconditional probability of $0.437$ is a population average of
two very different regimes, and no policy maker is ever standing in the unconditional
regime. They are always standing in one month, with one set of numbers in front of them,
which is exactly the conditioning problem Lecture 2 introduces with a regression in place
of a two-way split.

That is as far as splitting the sample by hand can go. A regression conditions on
continuous information rather than a single cutoff, a shrinkage prior conditions when
there are too many predictors to trust unregularised, and averaging over models conditions
on the fact that several regressions look equally defensible and disagree. Sections 5 and 6
run exactly that sequence, on this dataset, so that the last of it is not merely asserted:
by the end there is a genuine decision, which predictors to trust and how much, made while
admitting that the model itself is not known.

## The problem: model uncertainty is a variance term, not a footnote {#sec-problem}

### Result R-15.1: the variance a point estimate and a single model leave out

Let $y_\ast$ be a quantity of interest that depends on an unknown parameter vector
$\theta$ within a model $M$, and let $M$ itself be one of several candidate models. Applying
the law of total variance twice, once inside a model and once across models,

$$
\operatorname{Var}(y_\ast \mid y) =
\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_M\!\big[\operatorname{Var}(y_\ast \mid M, y)\big]}_{\text{averaged within-model variance}}
+ \underbrace{\operatorname{Var}_M\!\big[\mathbb{E}(y_\ast \mid M, y)\big]}_{\text{disagreement between models}},
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(y_\ast \mid M, y) =
\mathbb{E}_\theta\!\big[\operatorname{Var}(y_\ast \mid \theta, M, y)\big]
+ \operatorname{Var}_\theta\!\big[\mathbb{E}(y_\ast \mid \theta, M, y)\big].
$$

A procedure that fixes $\theta$ at a point estimate inside one chosen model reports only
the innermost term, $\operatorname{Var}(y_\ast \mid \theta, M, y)$, usually just an
estimated residual variance, and sets the other two terms to zero by construction. Nothing
in the mathematics licenses that; it is a choice, and the two omitted terms do not vanish
just because they are not reported.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

For any two random quantities $A$ and $B$, $\operatorname{Var}(A) =
\mathbb{E}_B[\operatorname{Var}(A \mid B)] + \operatorname{Var}_B[\mathbb{E}(A \mid B)]$,
by expanding $\operatorname{Var}(A) = \mathbb{E}[A^2] - \mathbb{E}[A]^2$ and conditioning
both terms on $B$. Apply this once with $A = y_\ast$ and $B = M$, conditioning throughout
on the data $y$, to get the outer decomposition. Apply it again inside the first term, now
with $A = y_\ast$ conditional on $M$ and $B = \theta$, to get the inner one. Both
applications are the same one-line identity; the only content here is applying it twice
rather than once.
:::

The two omitted terms are not exotic. The second, model disagreement, is the whole subject
of Lecture 9, and the sharper version of it, that not even every parameter within a model
is identified by the data, is the subject of Lectures 7 and 10. Fit two defensible
regressions for the inflation forecast of @sec-motivation on the same training data,
intercept, past inflation and the change in the funds rate in both, one of them adding the
unemployment rate.

```{python}
#| label: fig-problem-model-gap
#| fig-cap: "Two regressions that fit almost equally well in sample give forecasts that agree near the historical average unemployment rate and diverge by more than half a point at its extremes."
pred_c = ["infl_past", "unemp", "spread", "d_ff", "ipg", "y10"]
X_c = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(panel_c))] + [panel_c[c].to_numpy() for c in pred_c])
y_c = panel_c["infl_next"].to_numpy()
idx_c = panel_c.index
train_end = int(np.searchsorted(idx_c, pd.Timestamp("1989-01-01")))
X_train_c, y_train_c = X_c[:train_end], y_c[:train_end]

cols_A, cols_B = [0, 1, 2, 4], [0, 1, 4]        # +unemployment, and without it
beta_A, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X_train_c[:, cols_A], y_train_c, rcond=None)
beta_B, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X_train_c[:, cols_B], y_train_c, rcond=None)
resid_A = y_train_c - X_train_c[:, cols_A] @ beta_A
resid_B = y_train_c - X_train_c[:, cols_B] @ beta_B
n_tr, kA, kB = len(y_train_c), len(cols_A), len(cols_B)

means_tr = X_train_c.mean(axis=0)
u_grid = np.array([3.5, 5.0, 6.5, 8.0, 9.5])
pred_A = [float(np.array([1.0, means_tr[1], u, means_tr[4]]) @ beta_A) for u in u_grid]
pred_B = [float(np.array([1.0, means_tr[1], means_tr[4]]) @ beta_B) for _ in u_grid]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(u_grid, pred_A, "o-", color="C0", label="with unemployment")
ax.plot(u_grid, pred_B, "s--", color="C1", label="without unemployment")
ax.fill_between(u_grid, pred_A, pred_B, color="grey", alpha=0.25)
ax.axvline(panel_c["unemp"].mean(), color="black", lw=0.8, ls=":")
ax.set_xlabel("unemployment rate held at this value (%)")
ax.set_ylabel("forecast: inflation over the next 12 months (%)")
ax.legend(fontsize=9)
ax.set_title("Two models, one training sample, one disagreement")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"in-sample residual sd: with unemployment {np.sqrt(resid_A @ resid_A / (n_tr - kA)):.4f}, "
      f"without {np.sqrt(resid_B @ resid_B / (n_tr - kB)):.4f}")
print(f"forecast gap at unemployment = {u_grid[0]}: {pred_A[0] - pred_B[0]:.3f} points")
print(f"forecast gap at unemployment = {u_grid[-1]}: {pred_A[-1] - pred_B[-1]:.3f} points")
```

The two models fit the training sample almost identically, a residual standard deviation
of $1.076$ with unemployment in the equation against $1.093$ without it, so nothing in
sample forces a choice between them. Near the historical average unemployment rate of
about six percent the two forecasts agree to a few hundredths. Away from it, at an
unemployment rate of $3.5$ or $9.5$, they disagree by more than half a percentage point,
a gap comparable in size to the effect the whole shrinkage exercise of @sec-empirical will
have on this same forecast. A report that picked one of these two regressions and quoted
its residual standard deviation as the forecast uncertainty would never see that gap. It is
exactly the term $\operatorname{Var}_M[\mathbb{E}(y_\ast\mid M,y)]$ in R-15.1, and
@sec-methodology below gives it a name and a formula rather than leaving it as a picture.

The course met two further difficulties before this one, and it is worth being precise
about which is which. The first three lectures fought intractability: a posterior that
exists in principle but cannot be written down or integrated, repaired by simulation.
Lectures 6 through 9 fought estimation error: a posterior that can be written down but is
too noisy to trust once the parameter count approaches the sample size, repaired by a
prior that supplies the missing restrictions. This section's difficulty, and the one
Lectures 7, 10 and 11 spend the most effort on, is identification and model error, and it
is the one enemy this course only partly defeats. More data shrinks estimation error
essentially without limit; it does not, by itself, tell two structurally different but
equally well-fitting explanations of the same reduced-form residuals apart.

## Methodology: two repairs in general notation, and one that stays open {#sec-methodology}

Each of the course's difficulties has a general repair, and each repair is a different
one of the four objects from the Overview box doing new work. Intractability was repaired
by changing how the posterior is computed, from an integral to an average over simulated
draws, the subject of Lectures 3 to 5 and not revisited here since nothing about it is
specific to a review. Estimation error is repaired by changing the prior, and Result R-15.2
is the one behind every conjugate model in this course from Lecture 2 onward: it is what
makes the innermost variance term in R-15.1, the one a single fitted model reports on its
own, something to be computed exactly rather than merely estimated from a fixed formula.
Model uncertainty is repaired by changing which object answers the question at all, from a
single posterior predictive to a mixture of them, and Result R-15.3 is what turns the gap
of @fig-problem-model-gap from a picture into the middle term of R-15.1, with a weight
attached to each of the two disagreeing models rather than a shrug.

### Result R-15.2: the Normal-Inverse-Gamma posterior, for any $n$ and $k$

For $y = X\beta + \varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2 I_n)$,
$\beta \mid \sigma^2 \sim \mathcal N(b_0, \sigma^2 B_0)$ and
$\sigma^2 \sim \mathrm{IG}(\alpha_0, \delta_0)$, the posterior is exactly

$$
\beta \mid \sigma^2, y \sim \mathcal N(b_T, \sigma^2 B_T), \qquad
\sigma^2 \mid y \sim \mathrm{IG}(\alpha_T, \delta_T),
$$

$$
B_T = \big(B_0^{-1} + X^\top X\big)^{-1}, \qquad
b_T = B_T\big(B_0^{-1} b_0 + X^\top y\big), \qquad
\alpha_T = \alpha_0 + \tfrac{n}{2}, \qquad
\delta_T = \delta_0 + \tfrac12\big(y^\top y + b_0^\top B_0^{-1} b_0 - b_T^\top B_T^{-1} b_T\big),
$$

for any $n$, any $k$ and any design $X$, singular or not. Marginalising $\sigma^2$ gives a
Student predictive for a new observation at $x_\ast$,
$y_\ast \mid y \sim t_{2\alpha_T}\big(x_\ast^\top b_T,\, (\delta_T/\alpha_T)(1 + x_\ast^\top B_T x_\ast)\big)$,
in which the $1$ is the shock that hits regardless of how well $\beta$ is known and
$x_\ast^\top B_T x_\ast$ is exactly the innermost term of R-15.1, the part contributed by
not knowing $\beta$; it shrinks as the sample grows, the $1$ never does. Whenever $X^\top X$
is invertible, $b_T$ can be written as $W\hat\beta_{\mathrm{OLS}} + (I_k - W)b_0$ with
$W = (X^\top X/\sigma^2 + B_0^{-1})^{-1}(X^\top X/\sigma^2)$, a matrix whose eigenvalues lie
in $(0,1)$: the posterior mean is always a compromise between the prior and least squares,
weighted by precision, never a free choice of how much to trust either one.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

Drop constants and collect powers of $\beta$ in the log posterior, exactly as in Lecture 2:
the likelihood contributes $-(y-X\beta)^\top(y-X\beta)/2\sigma^2$ and the prior contributes
$-(\beta-b_0)^\top B_0^{-1}(\beta-b_0)/2\sigma^2$. Completing the square in $\beta$ gives
$B_T$ and $b_T$ as displayed, with the leftover constant term feeding directly into
$\delta_T$; matching this against an $\mathrm{IG}(\alpha_T,\delta_T)$ kernel in $\sigma^2$
identifies $\alpha_T$ and $\delta_T$. For the predictive, $y_\ast = x_\ast^\top\beta +
\varepsilon_\ast$ given $\sigma^2$ is $\mathcal N(x_\ast^\top b_T,\, \sigma^2(1+x_\ast^\top
B_T x_\ast))$, since $\beta\mid\sigma^2,y$ and $\varepsilon_\ast$ are independent Normals;
integrating $\sigma^2$ against its $\mathrm{IG}(\alpha_T,\delta_T)$ posterior is the same
scale-mixture calculation used for the Student-$t$ likelihood in Lectures 3 and 4, and
returns the displayed $t_{2\alpha_T}$ distribution. For the matrix-weighted form, substitute
$X^\top y = X^\top X\,\hat\beta_{\mathrm{OLS}}$ into $b_T$ and use $B_T B_0^{-1} = I_k - W$;
this is the same algebra as R-6.2, restated here for a general prior $B_0$ rather than the
Minnesota specialisation.
:::

R-15.2 is instanced differently every time it is used: a vague $B_0$ recovers ordinary
least squares up to a Bayesian wrapper, a Minnesota $B_0$ gives Lecture 6's shrinkage
across a whole vector autoregression, and a spike-and-slab prior in Lecture 11 puts the
same posterior mean inside each of exponentially many models rather than one. Every one of
these is the identical formula with a different $B_0$, which is the sense in which
estimation error has one repair, not fourteen.

### Result R-15.3: the model-averaged posterior predictive

Let $M_1,\dots,M_J$ be candidate models with prior probabilities $p(M_j)$ and let
$p(y\mid M_j)$ be model $j$'s marginal likelihood, $\int p(y\mid\theta_j,M_j)p(\theta_j\mid
M_j)\,d\theta_j$. The posterior model probabilities and the model-averaged predictive are

$$
p(M_j \mid y) = \frac{p(y\mid M_j)\,p(M_j)}{\sum_{i=1}^J p(y\mid M_i)\,p(M_i)},
\qquad
p(y_\ast \mid y) = \sum_{j=1}^J p(M_j \mid y)\, p(y_\ast \mid y, M_j),
$$

a mixture over models rather than a choice among them, with mean $\sum_j p(M_j\mid
y)\,\mathbb E(y_\ast\mid y,M_j)$ and variance given exactly by the two-term split of R-15.1,
the weighted average of the within-model variances plus the weighted variance of the
within-model means across $j$. A predictor's posterior inclusion probability, $\sum_{j:
\,\text{predictor}\in M_j} p(M_j\mid y)$, summarises how much of the model mass uses it at
all.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

Bayes' theorem applied to the discrete unknown $M$ gives $p(M_j\mid y) \propto p(y\mid
M_j)p(M_j)$, normalising over $j$ gives the displayed posterior model probability. The
posterior predictive marginalises both $\theta$ and $M$: $p(y_\ast\mid y) = \sum_j
p(y_\ast, M_j \mid y) = \sum_j p(y_\ast \mid y, M_j)\, p(M_j\mid y)$, which is the displayed
mixture. Its mean is $\mathbb E_M[\mathbb E(y_\ast\mid M,y)]$ by the tower property, and its
variance is R-15.1's outer decomposition read backwards: the same two terms that were
diagnosed as missing in @sec-problem are exactly the two terms this mixture supplies.
When each $M_j$ is a linear regression with an NIG prior, $p(y\mid M_j)$ is the closed form
of R-15.2's derivation with $\beta$ and $\sigma^2$ both integrated out, so R-15.2 and
R-15.3 use the same completed square twice, once per model and once across models.
:::

One difficulty is not repaired by either result. Identification asks whether the
parameters of a single, correctly specified model are pinned down by the data at all, and
R-15.2 and R-15.3 are both silent on it: they average or shrink across what the likelihood
can see, and a structural parameter the likelihood cannot see is invisible to both, however
many models are in the average. Lecture 7's reduced-form vector autoregression fits the
inflation, unemployment and policy-rate data as well as any structural model that could
generate it, and the residual covariance alone cannot say which of the many candidate maps
from those residuals to a monetary-policy shock is the right one; recursive ordering and
sign restrictions are extra assumptions bolted on from outside the likelihood, not
consequences of it. Lecture 10's potential-outcomes framework makes the same point about a
single treatment effect: no likelihood written on observed data alone can distinguish the
effect of a policy from the reasons the policy was chosen, and the course's causal chapter
spends its effort on stating assumptions precisely rather than on a sampler. R-15.2 and
R-15.3 both integrate over what the likelihood can see; a parameter the likelihood cannot
see stays exactly as unresolved after averaging over sixty-four models as after fitting
one. That is why this course carries three results and not four: two are general repairs,
and the third enemy's honest general statement is that more data is not always the answer.

## Data: core inflation and six predictors, 1961 to 2025 {#sec-data}

The chapter's one dataset is the monthly FRED macroeconomic panel used throughout
@sec-motivation, restricted to the six predictors used from here on: inflation over the
trailing twelve months, the unemployment rate, the term spread between the ten-year
Treasury yield and the federal funds rate, the change in the funds rate over the trailing
twelve months, industrial production growth over the trailing twelve months, and the level
of the ten-year yield. The target is core PCE inflation over the following twelve months.
Every predictor is observable at the forecast date; nothing in the panel looks into the
future.

```{python}
#| label: fig-data-panel
#| fig-cap: "Left: realised twelve-month-ahead core inflation over the full sample. Right: the correlation of each predictor, observed today, with inflation over the following year."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.5, 4.0))
axes[0].plot(panel_c.index, panel_c["infl_next"], lw=0.7, color="steelblue")
axes[0].axhline(3.0, color="black", lw=0.8, ls=":")
axes[0].set_ylabel("inflation, next 12 months (%)")
axes[0].set_title("Core inflation, one year ahead")

corr_c = panel_c.corr()["infl_next"].drop("infl_next")
axes[1].bar(range(len(corr_c)), corr_c.to_numpy(), color="steelblue")
axes[1].axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.8)
axes[1].set_xticks(range(len(corr_c))); axes[1].set_xticklabels(corr_c.index, rotation=30, fontsize=8)
axes[1].set_title("Correlation with next year's inflation")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"{len(panel_c)} months, {panel_c.index[0]:%Y-%m} to {panel_c.index[-1]:%Y-%m}")
print(panel_c.describe().loc[["mean", "std", "min", "max"]].round(2))
```

The transformed panel runs $774$ months, January 1961 to June 2025. Twelve-month-ahead
core inflation averages $3.22$ percent with a standard deviation of $2.00$, ranging from
$0.62$ to $9.73$; the trailing twelve-month figure that predicts it has almost the same
distribution, which is why persistence dominates everything else in the right-hand panel,
a correlation of $0.863$. The ten-year yield follows at $0.589$, the term spread at
$-0.450$, the change in the funds rate at $0.247$, unemployment at $0.126$, the wrong sign
for a textbook Phillips curve, and industrial production growth at essentially zero. The
sign on unemployment is a warning worth keeping in mind for @sec-empirical: an unconditional
correlation and a coefficient estimated alongside five other predictors are different
objects, and only one of them answers the question a forecaster actually asks. The
training window used throughout, January 1961 to December 1988, supplies $336$
observations for the first four steps below; the remaining months are held out for the
fifth.

## Empirical analysis: one forecast, five verdicts {#sec-empirical}

Everything above is now run on the panel of @sec-data, one method at a time, the same
question asked five times. Each step keeps the training window fixed at the $336$ months
ending December 1988 until the final step, which forecasts forward month by month using
only information available at each origin.

### Step one: the conjugate posterior in closed form

R-15.2 with a deliberately vague prior, $B_0 = 100\,I_7$, is the baseline: closed-form
Bayesian regression, barely distinguishable from ordinary least squares with this much
data relative to seven coefficients.

```{python}
from scipy.special import gammaln
from scipy import stats

alpha_0_c, delta_0_c = 3.0, 3.0

def nig_posterior(X, y, B0, b0=None):
    """R-15.2, in the course's b_0, B_0, alpha_0, delta_0 notation."""
    k = X.shape[1]
    b0 = np.zeros(k) if b0 is None else b0
    B0_inv = np.linalg.inv(B0)
    BT = np.linalg.inv(B0_inv + X.T @ X)
    bT = BT @ (B0_inv @ b0 + X.T @ y)
    aT = alpha_0_c + len(y) / 2
    dT = delta_0_c + 0.5 * (y @ y + b0 @ B0_inv @ b0 - bT @ np.linalg.inv(BT) @ bT)
    _, ld_BT = np.linalg.slogdet(BT)
    _, ld_B0 = np.linalg.slogdet(B0)
    lml = (gammaln(aT) - gammaln(alpha_0_c) + alpha_0_c * np.log(delta_0_c)
           - aT * np.log(dT) + 0.5 * (ld_BT - ld_B0) - 0.5 * len(y) * np.log(2 * np.pi))
    return bT, BT, aT, dT, lml

def student_predictive(x_star, bT, BT, aT, dT):
    return (float(x_star @ bT),
            float(np.sqrt((dT / aT) * (1 + x_star @ BT @ x_star))), 2 * aT)

names_c = ["intercept"] + pred_c
B0_vague = np.eye(7) * 100.0
bT1, BT1, aT1, dT1, lml1 = nig_posterior(X_train_c, y_train_c, B0_vague)
sd1 = np.sqrt((dT1 / (aT1 - 1)) * np.diag(BT1))

print(f"training sample: {len(y_train_c)} months, "
      f"{idx_c[0]:%Y-%m} to {idx_c[train_end - 1]:%Y-%m}")
print(pd.DataFrame({"post. mean": bT1, "post. sd": sd1}, index=names_c).round(4))
print(f"E[sigma^2 | y] = {dT1 / (aT1 - 1):.4f}, log marginal likelihood {lml1:.2f}")
```

Past inflation carries a posterior mean of $0.884$ with a posterior standard deviation of
only $0.043$, and unemployment, once six other things are held fixed, is negative at
$-0.155$, the Phillips-curve sign that the raw correlation of @sec-data hid. This is the
answer @sec-motivation's split-sample calculation was reaching for, now conditioning on all
six predictors at once instead of one cutoff.

### Step two: the same posterior by simulation

Nothing about the answer should depend on how it is computed, and checking that is the
discipline of Lectures 3 to 5. Draw directly from the closed-form posterior, and separately
run a Gibbs sampler for a model with an independent prior, $\beta \sim \mathcal N(0,
\tau_0^2 I)$, which is not jointly conjugate and genuinely needs the sampler.

```{python}
rng_c = np.random.default_rng(20260115)
S_c, burn_c = 8000, 1000

sig2_mc = stats.invgamma(a=aT1, scale=dT1).rvs(size=S_c, random_state=rng_c)
L_BT1 = np.linalg.cholesky(BT1)
beta_mc = bT1 + np.sqrt(sig2_mc)[:, None] * (rng_c.standard_normal((S_c, 7)) @ L_BT1.T)

tau0_c = 10.0
XtX_c, Xty_c = X_train_c.T @ X_train_c, X_train_c.T @ y_train_c
sig2_g, draws_g, sig2_g_draws = float(y_train_c.var()), np.empty((S_c, 7)), np.empty(S_c)
for s in range(S_c):
    Vg = np.linalg.inv(XtX_c / sig2_g + np.eye(7) / tau0_c ** 2)
    beta_g = Vg @ Xty_c / sig2_g + np.linalg.cholesky(Vg) @ rng_c.standard_normal(7)
    res_g = y_train_c - X_train_c @ beta_g
    sig2_g = float(stats.invgamma(a=alpha_0_c + len(y_train_c) / 2,
                                  scale=delta_0_c + 0.5 * res_g @ res_g).rvs(random_state=rng_c))
    draws_g[s], sig2_g_draws[s] = beta_g, sig2_g

print(pd.DataFrame({"closed form": bT1, "direct Monte Carlo": beta_mc[burn_c:].mean(axis=0),
                    "Gibbs, independent prior": draws_g[burn_c:].mean(axis=0)},
                   index=names_c).round(4))
print(f"E[sigma^2]: closed form {dT1 / (aT1 - 1):.4f}, "
      f"direct MC {sig2_mc[burn_c:].mean():.4f}, Gibbs {sig2_g_draws[burn_c:].mean():.4f}")
```

The three columns agree to within a few thousandths on every coefficient, and the two
routes to $\mathbb E[\sigma^2\mid y]$ agree to four figures, $1.1292$ against $1.1290$. That
is the check every sampler in this course exists to pass: with $336$ observations and a
near-flat prior, the algorithm used to reach the posterior does not change it, and neither
does swapping the prior for one with the same practical looseness. The point of running the
Gibbs sampler here at all, rather than only the direct draws, is that it would not agree by
construction if there were a coding error in either route, and it is the sampler, not the
closed form, that has to carry the argument once @sec-empirical's model average makes the
joint posterior of sixty-four different coefficient vectors too awkward to write down in
one line.

### Step three: a shrinkage prior

Take the shrinkage view instead: centre the six slopes at zero, $B_0 = c\,I$ on the slopes
with the intercept left vague, and let the marginal likelihood pick $c$ from a grid, exactly
R-15.2 with a different $B_0$.

```{python}
#| label: fig-shrinkage-evidence
#| fig-cap: "Log marginal likelihood against the shrinkage prior's tightness. The evidence favours a moderate amount of shrinkage over both extremes."
c_grid_c = [0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 10.0]

def B0_shrink(c):
    B = np.eye(7) * c
    B[0, 0] = 100.0
    return B

lmls_c = [nig_posterior(X_train_c, y_train_c, B0_shrink(c))[4] for c in c_grid_c]
c_star = c_grid_c[int(np.argmax(lmls_c))]
bT3, BT3, aT3, dT3, lml3 = nig_posterior(X_train_c, y_train_c, B0_shrink(c_star))
sd3 = np.sqrt((dT3 / (aT3 - 1)) * np.diag(BT3))

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(c_grid_c, lmls_c, "o-")
ax.axvline(c_star, color="firebrick", ls="--", lw=1, label=f"selected c = {c_star}")
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("prior variance c on each slope"); ax.set_ylabel("log marginal likelihood")
ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.set_title("Evidence against the tightness of the shrinkage prior")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"c = {c_star} selected; posterior mean on past inflation: {bT3[1]:.3f} "
      f"(vague prior gave {bT1[1]:.3f})")
```

The curve rises from $c=0.01$ to a maximum at $c=0.1$ and falls back beyond it, an interior
optimum rather than a monotone preference for more or less shrinkage, which is the same
U-shape R-6.1 derives for a vector autoregression. At $c^\ast = 0.1$ the coefficient on past
inflation moves only from $0.884$ to $0.870$; with $336$ observations and six predictors
there is not much estimation error left for a prior to remove. The contrast with Lecture 6
is instructive rather than accidental: there, $111$ coefficients competed for $120$
observations and shrinkage rewrote the fitted system almost completely; here, seven
coefficients have $336$ observations to themselves, and the same repair, applied to the
same kind of prior, has almost nothing left to do. R-15.2 does not know in advance which
situation it is in. It is the ratio of coefficients to observations, not the existence of a
prior, that decides how much a prior can still buy.

### Step four: averaging over which predictors belong

R-15.3 needs $p(y\mid M_j)$ for each of the $2^6 = 64$ subsets of the six predictors, few
enough to enumerate exactly rather than sample, each fitted with R-15.2 and a common vague
prior.

```{python}
combos_c = [tuple(j for j in range(6) if mask & (1 << j)) for mask in range(64)]

def bma_fit(X, y):
    lmls, posts = [], []
    for combo in combos_c:
        cols = [0] + [i + 1 for i in combo]
        out = nig_posterior(X[:, cols], y, np.eye(len(cols)) * 100.0)
        lmls.append(out[4]); posts.append((cols, out))
    lmls = np.array(lmls)
    wts = np.exp(lmls - lmls.max()); wts /= wts.sum()
    return wts, posts

w_bma, posts_bma = bma_fit(X_train_c, y_train_c)
pip_c = np.zeros(6)
for combo, wt in zip(combos_c, w_bma):
    for j in combo:
        pip_c[j] += wt
bT_bma = np.zeros(7)
for (cols, out), wt in zip(posts_bma, w_bma):
    bT_bma[cols] += wt * out[0]

order_c = np.argsort(-w_bma)[:3]
print("top three models by posterior probability")
for i in order_c:
    inc = [pred_c[j] for j in combos_c[i]]
    print(f"  {w_bma[i]:.3f}  {inc if inc else ['intercept only']}")
print("posterior inclusion probabilities:")
print(pd.Series(pip_c, index=pred_c).round(3))
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-coef-comparison
#| fig-cap: "The coefficient on each of the six predictors under the vague conjugate prior, the shrinkage prior, and model averaging. Bars are 90% credible intervals where a single model gives one."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 4.4))
offsets = [-0.22, 0.0, 0.22]
specs = [("vague conjugate", bT1, sd1, "C0"), (f"shrinkage, c={c_star}", bT3, sd3, "C1"),
         ("model averaged", bT_bma, None, "C2")]
pos_c = np.arange(6)
for off, (lbl, bb, ss, col) in zip(offsets, specs):
    ax.scatter(pos_c + off, bb[1:], color=col, s=34, label=lbl, zorder=3)
    if ss is not None:
        ax.vlines(pos_c + off, bb[1:] - 1.645 * ss[1:], bb[1:] + 1.645 * ss[1:], color=col, lw=1.6)
ax.axhline(0.0, color="black", lw=1.0, ls=":")
ax.set_xticks(pos_c); ax.set_xticklabels(pred_c, rotation=20)
ax.set_ylabel("coefficient on next year's inflation")
ax.set_title("What each treatment does to the same six coefficients")
ax.legend(fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Two of the sixty-four models carry almost all the mass, past inflation, unemployment and
the change in the funds rate at $0.597$, and the same pair without unemployment at $0.370$,
which is @fig-problem-model-gap's two regressions with their actual posterior weights
attached. Past inflation has a posterior inclusion probability of essentially $1$ and the
change in the funds rate $0.998$; the term spread, industrial production growth and the
long yield sit at $0.007$, $0.015$ and $0.013$. Averaging does not merely shrink the three
weak predictors, it multiplies each of them by the probability that it belongs at all,
moving the spread's coefficient from $-0.048$ under the vague prior to $-0.0002$ and the
long yield's from $-0.013$ to $-0.0007$, both far past where shrinkage alone had left them.
Unemployment keeps its negative sign under every treatment, $-0.155$, $-0.149$ and $-0.102$
in turn, the one coefficient in @fig-coef-comparison whose story does not change with the
method.

### Step five: does any of it forecast better?

The question that decides whether the last three steps were worth running. From January
1990, forecast month by month using only data whose twelve-month window had already
closed, and score against the historical mean of the training window as a benchmark that
uses no predictors at all.

```{python}
start_c = int(np.searchsorted(idx_c, pd.Timestamp("1990-01-01")))
oos_c = []
for t in range(start_c, len(y_c)):
    end = t - 12
    Xs, ys, x_star = X_c[:end], y_c[:end], X_c[t]
    m1, s1, df1 = student_predictive(x_star, *nig_posterior(Xs, ys, B0_vague)[:4])
    best = max((nig_posterior(Xs, ys, B0_shrink(c)) for c in c_grid_c), key=lambda o: o[4])
    m2, s2, df2 = student_predictive(x_star, *best[:4])
    wts, posts = bma_fit(Xs, ys)
    ms = np.array([student_predictive(x_star[cols], *out[:4])[0] for cols, out in posts])
    ss = np.array([student_predictive(x_star[cols], *out[:4])[1] for cols, out in posts])
    m3 = float(wts @ ms)
    s3 = float(np.sqrt(wts @ ss ** 2 + wts @ (ms - m3) ** 2))
    oos_c.append((idx_c[t], y_c[t], m1, s1, df1, m2, s2, df2, m3, s3, ys.mean(), ys.std()))

O = pd.DataFrame(oos_c, columns=["date", "y", "m1", "s1", "df1", "m2", "s2", "df2",
                                 "m3", "s3", "hm", "hs"]).set_index("date")

def score_c(m, s, df=None):
    rmse = float(np.sqrt(np.mean((O.y - m) ** 2)))
    lps = (float(np.mean(stats.norm.logpdf(O.y, m, s))) if df is None else
           float(np.mean(stats.t.logpdf((O.y - m) / s, df=df) - np.log(s))))
    return rmse, lps

scores = pd.DataFrame(
    [score_c(O.hm, O.hs), score_c(O.m1, O.s1, O.df1), score_c(O.m2, O.s2, O.df2), score_c(O.m3, O.s3)],
    columns=["OOS RMSE", "OOS log score"],
    index=["historical mean", "conjugate", "shrinkage", "model averaged"])

what_changed = pd.DataFrame({
    "what it adds": ["nothing, a benchmark", "R-15.2, closed form", "R-15.2, prior shrinks slopes",
                     "R-15.3, mixture over 64 models"],
    "unemployment coef.": [np.nan, bT1[2], bT3[2], bT_bma[2]],
    "OOS RMSE": scores["OOS RMSE"].to_numpy(), "OOS log score": scores["OOS log score"].to_numpy(),
}, index=["0 benchmark", "1 conjugate", "2 shrinkage", "3 model averaged"])

print(f"{len(O)} out-of-sample months, {O.index[0]:%Y-%m} to {O.index[-1]:%Y-%m}")
print(what_changed.round(4).to_string())
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-cumulative-score
#| fig-cap: "Cumulative log predictive score relative to the no-predictor benchmark, month by month from January 1990. All three methods stay ahead throughout."
adv = pd.DataFrame({
    "conjugate": stats.t.logpdf((O.y - O.m1) / O.s1, df=O.df1) - np.log(O.s1) - stats.norm.logpdf(O.y, O.hm, O.hs),
    "shrinkage": stats.t.logpdf((O.y - O.m2) / O.s2, df=O.df2) - np.log(O.s2) - stats.norm.logpdf(O.y, O.hm, O.hs),
    "model averaged": stats.norm.logpdf(O.y, O.m3, O.s3) - stats.norm.logpdf(O.y, O.hm, O.hs),
}, index=O.index).cumsum()

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for col, colour in zip(adv.columns, ["C0", "C1", "C2"]):
    ax.plot(adv.index, adv[col], color=colour, lw=1.4, label=col)
ax.axhline(0.0, color="black", lw=1.0, ls=":")
ax.set_xlabel("forecast date"); ax.set_ylabel("cumulative log score minus the benchmark's")
ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.set_title("Every step beats the benchmark; not every step beats the last one")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(adv.iloc[-1].round(2))
```

The table is the chapter's whole argument compressed into four rows. Row 0, the historical
mean, is the Lecture 1 answer with no conditioning at all and forecasts worst by a wide
margin, an out-of-sample root mean squared error of $1.917$ against $0.955$ or better for
every conditioned model. Row 1, R-15.2 with a vague prior, does almost all of the work by
itself, which is unsurprising with $336$ or more training months and only seven
coefficients; row 2's shrinkage prior improves the root mean squared error only from
$0.955$ to $0.952$, a fraction of one percent, because there was little estimation error
left to remove. Row 3, model averaging, is the one row that makes things slightly worse
out of sample, $0.967$ against $0.955$, even though it commanded the largest posterior
weight in sample. The reason is visible in @fig-coef-comparison: averaging pushed the term
spread, industrial production growth and the long yield close enough to zero that the
$36$-year holdout, which the training window never saw, occasionally needed them back, and
a marginal likelihood computed on data ending in 1989 cannot know that. All three
conditioned methods stay ahead of the benchmark for the entire $36$ years in
@fig-cumulative-score, ending $286.68$, $288.06$ and $283.25$ log points ahead for the
conjugate, shrinkage and model-averaged forecasts respectively; the ranking among the three
never reverses in the picture, which is a stronger statement than the single final number.
Model averaging is a genuine repair for the difficulty R-15.1 names, but repairing that
difficulty and forecasting best are not the same achievement, and this dataset is small and
tame enough that the difference barely shows.

## Discussion: what is settled, and what stays a judgement {#sec-discussion}

Every conditioned method beat a forecast that used no predictors at all, by a wide and
stable margin over thirty-six years; that is the least surprising and most important
result in @sec-empirical, because it is the one that would have made the whole exercise
pointless had it come out the other way. Within the conditioned methods, the ranking is
more honest than flattering to any one repair. The plain conjugate posterior of R-15.2 did
almost all of the work, the shrinkage prior added a sliver more, and model averaging, the
repair for exactly the difficulty diagnosed in R-15.1, was the one method that forecast
slightly worse than committing to a single well-chosen model. That is not a contradiction
of R-15.1 or R-15.3; both are statements about what a procedure accounts for, not
guarantees that accounting for more always forecasts better on any particular sample.
Lecture 6's reading, that dense shrinkage usually beats sparse selection on economic data
because most modest predictors carry a little information rather than none, is the same
lesson seen from the other side here: this panel had only six candidate predictors and
three hundred or more observations, so there was very little sparsity for model averaging
to correctly discover, and its confidence in the small model was, on this holdout, slightly
misplaced.

The map below is not new content, only a different arrangement of everything the course
already did, organised by what each lecture contributed rather than by week number.


Placed this way, a question that hands you a prior and a likelihood and asks for a
posterior is testing the first two columns; a question that says the full conditional is
not standard is testing the third; a question about what an investor should do, or whether
a forecast was any good, is testing the fourth. What is settled, in the sense of having a
general result that applies whatever the model, is the first three columns: R-15.2 gives
the posterior for any conjugate model, and Lectures 3 to 5 give a computational route when
it is not conjugate. The fourth column is only partly settled. Model averaging in R-15.3 is
as general as R-15.2, but which models to average over, what prior probability to give each
one, and what a decision maker's objective is once the predictive distribution is in hand,
are judgements the mathematics does not make for you. This chapter has no next lecture to
point to; what it can honestly say is that the identification difficulty of Lectures 7 and
10 is where that judgement is hardest, and that a forecaster who has internalised R-15.1,
that a single number always hides a variance term, has learned the one habit from this
course most likely to survive contact with a dataset it was never trained on.

## Exercises

These are the chapter's practice questions; the [Week 15 exercise
session](../exercise-sessions/15-review.qmd) works through them and adds the lab.

1. By hand. Prove the two-line identity behind R-15.1, $\operatorname{Var}(A) =
   \mathbb E_B[\operatorname{Var}(A\mid B)] + \operatorname{Var}_B[\mathbb E(A\mid B)]$,
   from the definition of variance, then specialise it to two models with posterior
   probabilities $w$ and $1-w$ and means $\mu_1 \ne \mu_2$, showing that the between-model
   term equals $w(1-w)(\mu_1-\mu_2)^2$. Evaluate it for the two models of
   @fig-problem-model-gap at an unemployment rate of $9.5$ using the posterior weights of
   @sec-empirical's step four, and compare it with the within-model term at the same point.

2. Computational. Recompute @sec-empirical's shrinkage grid with the intercept given the
   same prior variance as the slopes instead of a vague one, and report whether $c^\ast$
   and the selected coefficients move. Then extend the model-averaging enumeration to
   eight predictors by adding two further lags of core inflation, and report whether the
   two leading models of step four survive.

3. On real data. Repeat the five steps of @sec-empirical with headline CPI inflation in
   place of core PCE inflation as the target, keeping the same six predictors and the same
   training window. Report whether the ranking of the four rows in the out-of-sample table
   changes, and say in one paragraph whether the answer depends on which price index a
   central bank happens to target.

## Reading and references

R-15.2 is the Normal-Inverse-Gamma machinery of Lecture 2, restated for general $B_0$; its
shrinkage reading follows Lecture 6 and, ultimately, UPM Class 5 and SGPE Lecture 4. R-15.3
follows Lecture 9's treatment of Bayesian model averaging and posterior predictive mixtures.
The lesson that dense shrinkage often forecasts better than the sparse selection that model
averaging can produce, visible in @sec-empirical's step five, is examined directly in
Giannone, Lenza and Primiceri (2021), already cited in Lecture 6. Structural identification
and causal inference, this chapter's one unrepaired difficulty, have their own reading lists
in Lectures 7 and 10; consult those chapters directly rather than this one for the sources
behind that argument.

The explanations and exercises are adapted to this course's notation and weekly structure;
consult the cited originals for the full treatments.

Koop, *Bayesian Econometrics*, ch. 1-4. Chan, Koop, Poirier and Tobias, *Bayesian
Econometric Methods* (2nd ed.), ch. 1-4. Gelman et al., *Bayesian Data Analysis* (3rd ed.,
2013). Giannone, Lenza and Primiceri (2021), "Economic Predictions with Big Data: The
Illusion of Sparsity," *Econometrica*.
